title: Changes in and Stability of Well-Being During Adolescence:  A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Studies Over Two Decades
description: In this meta-analytic review, we examine the development of well-being during adolescence by synthesizing mean-level changes and rank-order stability in longitudinal studies. We conceptualize well-being as a multidimensional construct that includes hedonic well-being, eudaimonic well-being, and quality of life. To compute effect sizes, we used the standardized mean change d per year and test-retest correlations adjusted for measurement error. Analyses of the mean-level change were based on 502 effect sizes from a total of 551,009 adolescents. Analyses of the rank-order stability were based on 427 effect sizes from a total of 515,081 adolescents. The results showed that well-being declines every year (d ̅_year = −.03) and the cumulative decline during adolescence is d= -.27. The rank-order stability is high (r ̅ = .62). Only the linear function of age was positively related to rank-order stability. Moderator analyses showed that the findings for mean-level changes and rank-order stability were consistent across gender, birth cohort, ethnicity, economic development of the country, concepts of well-being, positive and negative aspects of well-being, and the quality of studies. Time interval length was negatively associated with rank-order stability. The subgroup analysis of the positive and negative aspects of well-being revealed that younger generations born after 2000 are more likely to experience greater declines in well-being. In sum, well-being tends to decline during adolescence, yet well-being is stable. These findings provide a clear and precise picture of the changes in well-being and the stability of well-being during adolescence.

title: Participation Effects in Ecological Momentary Assessment Research: A Taxonomy and Call to Action
description:
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) is often praised for its ecological validity, under the assumption that change observed in EMA data reflects change in the underlying constructs, independent of study participation. However, participation itself may threaten ecological validity as participants’ involvement in an EMA study may already alter their experiences, behavior or responses. Existing research on such participation effects has primarily documented their occurrence rather than explained the mechanisms through which they arise. To advance this understanding, we developed a taxonomy of potential sources of (measurement-induced) change in EMA data. This taxonomy includes increased reflection on assessed constructs (i.e., measurement reactivity), alterations to daily routines (i.e., measurement interference), shifts in how participants interpret items or response scales (i.e., reconceptualization or recalibration), practice in gauging internal states (i.e., improved introspection), and declining participant engagement (i.e., heightened careless responding or reduced compliance). Identifying these distinct sources of change highlights the need for systematic investigation of their impact and the development of targeted mitigation strategies. We therefore outline a research agenda focusing on assessing and experimentally manipulating each source of measurement-induced change in isolation. In sum, this paper aims to initiate a collective effort among EMA researchers to clarify the mechanisms by which study participation shapes data, and to safeguard EMA’s promise of ecological validity. 

Keywords: experience sampling methodology, measurement reactivity, (ecological) validity, response shifts, careless or insufficient effort responding

title: Impairment in the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology
description:
The purpose of this paper is to define and describe impairment from the perspective of the
Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP). This work is intended to establish a
foundation for the development of a system for assessing impairment to complement HiTOP
measures of psychopathology. We define impairment as the direct or indirect impact of
psychopathology that is not itself part of psychopathology, involving (a) difficulty achieving
important and reasonable personal goals and/or (b) direct or indirect interference with the goals
of others. We articulate seven specific assessment features of a HiTOP-optimal impairment
measurement approach and, having found no existing measures with all seven features in a
review of the literature, sketch a prototype approach using a case example and outline a plan
for generating a suite of tools for assessing impairment from a HiTOP perspective.

title: Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater! Why "preregistration" is still a useful term: Commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)
description: This is a commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025), published in Avances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science (AMPPS). As per AMPPS submission guidelines, no abstract is included for commentaries.

title: Laughing Together Influences Neural Synchrony in Child Peers: An fNIRS Hyperscanning Study
description: Shared laughter, a salient social cue in peer interactions, promotes bonding, liking and prosociality. Recent theoretical accounts on the neural dynamics of social interaction propose that rhythmic communicative signals, such as laughter, may foster neural synchrony by aligning brain activities between interacting partners, facilitating mutual understanding and social bonding. Here, we test whether neural synchrony mediates the positive social effects of laughing together in child peer dyads. We used fNIRS hyperscanning to measure neural synchrony in 5-year-old dyads (n = 196; 98 pairs) randomly assigned to a laughter condition (funny animal videos) or a control condition (neutral videos). Inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and temporoparietal junction (TPJ) activity was recorded both during the video manipulation and during a subsequent 5-minute free-play session, and quantified with Wavelet Transform Coherence. Laughter behavior was annotated, bonding indexed by body proximity, prosociality with a sticker sharing task, and liking with smiley scales. Hypotheses were tested with Bayesian models. Compared with controls, children in the laughter condition showed higher neural synchrony while co-watching the videos. During free play, after the manipulation, left-hemisphere synchrony was greater in the control group. Exploratory findings showed that more laughter was linked to stronger bonding and prosociality. We did not find support for a mediation between laughter, neural synchrony and social outcomes. In summary, we show that neural synchrony among children changes with shared laughter. By revealing condition-specific and region-specific effects across time, this study highlights the dynamic nature of neural synchrony processes in child peer interactions.

title: Measuring Autistic Burnout: Psychometric Properties of the Autistic Burnout Severity Items in French
description: Autistic burnout is increasingly recognized in the literature, yet no validated French-language measure existed. This study examined the psychometric properties of a French adaptation of the Autistic Burnout Severity Items (ABSI-Fr) in a sample of autistic adults with lived experience of burnout (N = 393, drawn from a larger sample of 484). Exploratory factor analysis (polychoric correlations, minres extraction, Promax rotation) identified a six-factor, 26-item structure spanning exhaustion, social withdrawal, memory, cognitive slowing, autistic self-awareness, and emotional/somatic distress, differing from the original four-factor ABSI and from existing measures of autistic burnout. Internal consistency was satisfactory (α = .694-.867; ω = .646-.809), and a Schmid-Leiman transformation supported a hierarchical structure justifying both total and subscale scores (ωH = .762, ECV = .47, PUC = .852). The total score correlated significantly with depression, anxiety, general burnout, camouflaging, and alexithymia, albeit modestly, and was not significantly associated with autistic traits (AQ-10). The structure replicated closely in the full sample (N = 484). These findings provide the first evidence for a reliable, multidimensional measure of autistic burnout in French, offering French-speaking clinicians and autistic communities a tool to name and assess this experience; diagnostic thresholds are addressed in a companion paper.

title: Far out: How to achieve extreme results without really trying
description:
Extremism – political or otherwise – presupposes the presence of extreme, unusual, unexpected, or
outlying numerical values on some scale, and likewise, extreme judgments about such values.
Political extremism is the paradigmatic domain in which pertinent psychological dynamics play out.
Extremism is commonly considered undesirable, and to explain it, it is routine to invoke similarly
undesirable psychological constructs, as amply demonstrated in many chapters in this volume. In
this chapter, we show that fundamental perceptual, statistical, and behavioral mechanisms can
produce extreme results no one foresaw, intended, or desired. We further show that extreme results
can occur without the contribution of comparative perceptual or judgmental processes.

title: Spatial and featural cue weighting in children’s developing object representations
description: To accurately represent an object, observers must individuate it from surrounding objects and classify it with the appropriate category or identity. Adults flexibly weight different visual cues when perceiving objects, but less is known about whether, and how, the weighting of visual object information changes over development. The current study examined how and why children weight spatial (e.g., left/right location) and featural (e.g., color) cues during object perception. In Experiment 1, we tested whether 12-month-old infants and 4-year-old children encoded spatial and featural properties of objects, and, importantly, how children weighted these cues when they were pitted against each other. Infants learned and used relative spatial position more reliably than featural information. By contrast, preschoolers encoded both types of information but weighted featural information more heavily when the cues conflicted. In Experiment 2, we used computational models to test whether different visual objectives—individuation versus classification—are sufficient to produce these patterns of cue weighting. Models trained to individuate objects weighted spatial information more than features, whereas models trained to classify object weighted featural information more than space. These findings suggest that developmental changes in spatial and featural weighting may reflect, in part, changes in the visual objectives that guide object perception.

title: Pathways to Autistic Burnout: A Qualitative Study of French Autistic Adults' Experiences
description:
Purpose: Autistic burnout—a state of chronic exhaustion with functional loss and increased sensory sensitivity—has been identified as a significant yet underexplored phenomenon. While emerging research has documented potential contributors in Anglophone contexts, little is known about how autistic individuals in diverse institutional settings describe pathways to burnout. This study examined how French autistic adults identify and articulate factors contributing to their experiences of autistic burnout.
Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 67 French autistic adults (48 women, 11 men, 8 non-binary/agender/genderfluid; mean age 37.7 years; mean age at diagnosis 35.2 years). Interviews explored perceived contributors to burnout and were analyzed using qualitative content analysis with an abductive approach.
Results: Participants described burnout as emerging from cumulative exposure to unaccommodating environments rather than discrete triggering events. Key contributors included persistent sensory overload, social demands requiring sustained self-monitoring, camouflaging, and systemic barriers to recognition and support. Participants emphasized how chronic adaptation progressively depleted resources, with life transitions or micro-disruptions functioning as tipping points within already fragile equilibriums. Gendered experiences, particularly late diagnosis linked to gender-biased diagnostic frameworks, intensified burnout pathways for women and gender-diverse individuals.
Conclusion: Autistic burnout reflects sustained adaptation to environments misaligned with autistic needs rather than individual deficit. Findings underscore the need for multilevel interventions addressing environmental barriers, reducing camouflaging pressures, and ensuring timely, accessible diagnostic and support systems. France's distinctive institutional landscape—marked by psychoanalytic legacies and diagnostic delays—may shape how universal burnout mechanisms manifest.

title: When ‘Us’ Matters Less: Social Identity Complexity and Reduced Ingroup Favoritism in Stereotyping
description: How do people’s own identity structures shape the way they stereotype others? Across two preregistered experiments using a free-response stereotyping task and valence analysis, we tested whether social identity complexity (the extent to which individuals view their ingroups as differentiated rather than overlapping) was associated with intergroup bias in spontaneous stereotype valence. Consistent with classic intergroup patterns, participants generated more positive stereotypes for targets who shared more of their social group memberships. Social identity complexity moderated this bias by reducing the positivity of ingroup stereotypes rather than by enhancing evaluations of outgroup targets. To illuminate this process, we examined two potential mechanisms: ingroup attachment and perceived diagnosticity of social categories. Results aligned with an indirect effect through lower ingroup attachment, but not through perceived diagnosticity. These findings show that perceivers’ representations of their own social identities meaningfully shape how they spontaneously stereotype others, primarily by reducing ingroup favoritism.

title: Does Authenticity Matter in Humor Appreciation?
description: Does authenticity matter in a domain where one’s words and persona aren’t meant to be taken at face value? People often say “I’m just joking” to mean “Don’t take my words or actions literally.” To date, little is known about the role of authenticity in humor appreciation. To explore this question, we used audio recordings of comedic stories told by standup comedians (Experiments 1-3), text-only comedic stories (Experiments 4 & 6), and text-only observational jokes (Experiment 5) as comedic materials. We manipulated perceptions of authenticity by alleging the comedian prioritizes authentic self-expression (vs. pleasing their audience) (Experiment 1), performs because they love performing (vs. for fame and money) (Experiment 2), tells jokes that are based on real, personal (vs. fictional, imagined) experiences (Experiments 3 & 6), or wrote their own jokes (vs. used another human writer or AI) (Experiments 4-5). Across all studies, people evaluated the allegedly authentic jokes as funnier and expressed greater interest in following or sharing the comedian’s work.

title: Social Network Centrality and Emotional Dynamics in Classroom Learning: A Multilevel Approach
description:
Background: Students' emotions are shaped both by the structure of their peer relationships and by the affective context of the classroom. Two features of a student's position in the classroom network may matter: being sought out by peers (in-degree centrality), indexing social acceptance, and reaching out to many peers (out-degree centrality), indexing the breadth of active peer engagement. Classroom emotional climate, the aggregated activated affect of the class, may further shape these associations. Yet few studies have examined how a student's network position and the surrounding climate jointly relate to emotional experience.
Aims: We examined how in-degree and out-degree centrality relate to students' emotions across four dimensions (positive and negative, activated and deactivated) and whether classroom emotional climate (aggregated positive or negative activated affect) moderates these relationships.
Sample: Data were collected from 1,284 high school students (50.5% female, Mage = 16.26, SD = 0.88) nested within 56 classrooms.
Methods: We used multilevel structural equation modelling.
Results: Higher out-degree centrality was associated with lower positive activated and lower positive deactivated affect. Higher in-degree centrality was associated with higher positive deactivated affect and with lower negative activated and lower negative deactivated affect. Classroom emotional climate moderated several of these associations: a positive climate attenuated the negative association between out-degree centrality and positive affect, whereas a negative climate weakened the protective association between in-degree centrality and lower negative affect.
Conclusions: Students' network positions were differentially associated with their emotions, and these associations depended on the classroom's emotional climate.

title: Childhood maltreatment, brain development, and psychiatric risk
description: Childhood maltreatment impacts brain development in ways that vary by adversity type, developmental timing, and genetic vulnerability for psychiatric illness—heterogeneity that conventional approaches poorly capture. We contend that normative modeling, multivariate methods, and polygenic risk scores offer complementary frameworks for parsing this variability, advancing both mechanistic insight and clinical stratification.
